title: The soul's self-harm
hookLine: the soul harms itself most when it turns against others in anger (Meditations 2.16)

lines: IF IT'S HEAVY: 988, OR LOCAL HELP.
cards: There's an old saying, often repeated and of uncertain origin, that holding a grudge is like drinking poison and waiting for the other person to get sick. Marcus never heard it, but his notebook circles the same idea.
In section sixteen he lists the ways a soul wounds itself, and one of them is anger. A word first: Marcus means this as a picture of what anger and falseness do inside us.
If the phrase self-harm touches something painful in your own life, please reach out to someone you trust today. In the US, call or text 988, any hour; elsewhere, local emergency help.

teach.h: FIVE WAYS THE SOUL HURTS ITSELF.
teach.b: First, the claim. The soul does violence to itself, Marcus says, and he names five ways. The striking thing is the direction.
Harm usually means something done to you. Marcus is interested in the harm done from the inside.

teach.h: RAGING LIKE A GROWTH ON THE WORLD.
teach.b: Second, a growth on the world.

The first way is when the soul becomes, in his image, like a swelling or a tumor on the universe: when it rages against whatever happens, as if it could pull away from the whole of nature it belongs to.
Third, turning against others. The second way: when the soul turns away from another person, or moves against them meaning to hurt them, the way angry people do.
Marcus's point is that anger at someone else wounds the one who carries it. People were made, he said earlier in this book, to work together, like two hands.
A hand that strikes the other hand hurts the body it belongs to.

Fourth, masks and aimlessness. The other ways: when the soul is overpowered by pleasure or pain; when it plays a part, saying or doing anything false; and when it acts with no aim at all, carelessly, without thinking.
All five are harms done from inside.
And that's practical: if the harm comes from inside, so can the repair. A grudge softened by one degree is one less wound.

how: Some people practicing Stoicism treat anger and resentment as harms to their own character first, and work to loosen grudges for that reason.

o: Marcus's image for a soul raging against what happens
a curse an angry person sends to harm an enemy
a sickness Marcus suffered in his chest and stomach

games.q: the soul's self-harm — tap the pairs.

s: Marcus says anger mostly harms the person you're angry at
his point is that it wounds the soul that carries it.
Marcus counts saying or doing something false as one of the soul's self-harms
Marcus says the soul is harmed most by what others do to it
the entry is about harm done from the inside.

games.q: someone wronged you months ago. you still replay it daily. what does Meditations 2.16 suggest about who's being hurt?
o: you: turning against someone in anger wounds your own soul.
games.why: Marcus lists turning against another in anger as a way the soul does violence to itself.

practice: Bring to mind one grudge you're carrying, not the biggest, a medium one, and notice where it lives in your body: jaw, chest, stomach. Without excusing anything they did, breathe into that place and let it soften by one degree.
You're not doing this for them; you're putting down a little of what you've been carrying.

wordCard.voice: Tumor. Marcus's image for a soul that rages against what happens, as if it could pull away from the whole of nature it belongs to. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: don't harm myself. A surprisingly kind way to say: let it go a little. Day five hundred thirty-eight, done.
